question: Renal ultrasound in a 65-year-old man with AKI shows bilateral kidneys of 8.5 cm length with increased cortical echogenicity and loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Which finding on ultrasound would MOST change your management acutely?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bilateral hydronephrosis indicates post-renal (obstructive) AKI and demands immediate urological decompression. This finding completely redirects acute management — it is the most actionable ultrasound finding in AKI.

Small kidneys support chronicity (CKD) but do not change immediate acute management in the same urgent way as hydronephrosis. They inform prognosis and long-term planning rather than requiring an emergency intervention.

Increased cortical echogenicity suggests parenchymal disease (CKD, glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy) but does not mandate an immediate change in acute management. It is an informative, not an urgent-action, finding.

answers.text: Normal kidney size with preserved corticomedullary differentiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Normal size and differentiation support acute injury (AKI) rather than chronicity — useful for establishing acuity but does not change management as urgently as hydronephrosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bilateral hydronephrosis identifies reversible obstructive AKI requiring immediate urological decompression. Other ultrasound findings inform classification and prognosis but do not mandate an emergency procedural intervention.

Correct. Bilateral hydronephrosis = post-renal obstruction = urgent urological intervention. This is the most actionable ultrasound finding — all other findings inform prognosis but do not require immediate procedural management.
